planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to early fall directly into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, setting the rhizome shallowly with its top at or just below the soil surface.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or early fall directly into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, setting the rhizome shallowly with its top at or barely below the surface in partial shade to full sun. Iris nelsonii, called the Abbeville iris, is a naturally occurring Louisiana iris species found historically in only a handful of roadside ditches near Abbeville, Louisiana, believed to have arisen from natural crossing among copper iris, giant blue iris, and zigzag iris. Its branched flower stalks carry brick-red to deep maroon-red blooms held above sword-shaped foliage in mid-spring, attracting bumblebees and swallowtail butterflies. Because wild populations are so geographically limited, growing nursery-propagated plants in a wet Gulf Coast rain garden or pond margin adds a flower color unmatched by any other native iris while easing pressure on the rare wild colonies.

planting.note: Establish from nursery plugs in spring in full sun in dry, sandy, infertile, well-drained soil; wiregrass is the dominant native groundcover grass of longleaf pine flatwoods and savannas across the Gulf Coastal Plain.

directions: Establish from container-grown plugs in spring in full sun in lean, sandy, well-drained soil, since wiregrass struggles in rich or poorly drained ground. This fine-textured, wiry bunchgrass forms tight blue-green clumps and sends up slender flowering stalks in fall that catch afternoon light beautifully, echoing the look of the longleaf pine savannas it dominates across the Gulf Coastal Plain. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and historically depended on periodic fire to flower and reseed, so gardeners typically cut clumps back hard in late winter to mimic that cycle. Use it in sandy, low-fertility beds, native plant meadows, or pine-savanna-style landscaping where showier, moisture-loving grasses would fail.

common_name: Prairie Rose Gentian (Texas Star, Meadow Pink)

planting.note: Direct sow seed on the soil surface in fall in full sun in moist, open, disturbed ground; seedlings overwinter as small rosettes and bloom the following late spring into summer, typical of many Gulf Coast prairie annuals.

directions: Direct sow seed on bare, disturbed soil in fall since seeds need light and cold-season moisture to germinate; plants overwinter as low rosettes and shoot up the following spring in full sun and evenly moist, open ground. Prairie rose gentian is a slender, branching annual wildflower of Gulf Coast prairies, roadsides, and open meadows from Texas through Louisiana, bearing bright pink, five-petaled, star-shaped flowers with a greenish-yellow eye that open through late spring and summer. Bees and small butterflies visit the flowers readily, and plants reseed freely once established, making them a low-maintenance addition to a wildflower meadow or naturalized prairie planting. Because it thrives in the same lean, seasonally moist soils common across the Gulf Coast, it pairs well with other native prairie annuals without needing supplemental fertility.

common_name: Coastal Plain St. John's-Wort (Atlantic St. John's-Wort)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; this species grows naturally in seasonally flooded pine savannas, wet flatwoods, and pond edges across the Gulf Coastal Plain.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to light shade, mimicking the seasonally flooded pine flatwoods and pond margins where it grows wild. This small, upright, semi-evergreen shrub has fine, needle-like leaves and produces a summer-long succession of bright yellow flowers with a prominent tuft of stamens at each branch tip, attracting native bees and other small pollinators. It tolerates standing water for extended periods yet also handles the seasonal dry-down typical of Gulf Coast wet pinelands, making it a resilient choice for the fluctuating water levels of a rain garden or pond-edge planting. Use it as a filler shrub among taller wetland trees or massed along a ditch or bioswale where few other woody plants can establish.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

common_name: Fiddleleaf Morning Glory (White Beach Morning Glory)

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed, or set out rooted cuttings, after the last frost into loose, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; this trailing dune vine tolerates salt spray, wind, and shifting sand better than almost any other flowering ground cover.

directions: Direct sow scarified seed or root stem cuttings after the last frost in loose, well-drained sandy soil in full sun, watering only to establish since the vine is adapted to droughty dune sand. Fiddleleaf morning glory sends out long, prostrate, fleshy stems lined with distinctive lobed, fiddle-shaped leaves and opens white, funnel-shaped flowers with a soft yellow throat through the warm months. It is a close coastal relative of the pink-flowered railroad vine, and its network of trailing stems and deep roots make it an effective, low-growing sand stabilizer for beachfront and other extremely sandy, salt-exposed Gulf Coast sites. Because it spreads by rooting at the nodes, it also works well cascading over a hot, dry retaining wall or bank where little else will grow.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade along pond margins, wet ditches, or bog garden edges across the Gulf Coastal Plain.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, siting them along a pond edge, wet ditch, or bog garden bed where the roots stay damp. This slender native shrub takes its name from its narrow, whorled leaves that resemble bedstraw (Galium), and it produces cheerful bright yellow, five-petaled flowers with showy stamens through the summer months. It grows naturally in wet pine savannas, pond-cypress depressions, and roadside ditches from the Gulf Coast into the Southeast, tolerating both standing water and periodic dry spells once its roots are established. Its fine texture and steady summer bloom make it a useful, low-maintenance shrub for softening the edges of a rain garden or wetland planting while feeding native bees.

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a sturdy arbor or fence in well-drained sandy soil in full sun; this small, thin-barked native grape of Florida and the Gulf Coast is far more heat- and drought-tolerant than most cultivated bunch grapes.

directions: Plant dormant cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a sturdy arbor, fence, or large shrub in well-drained sandy soil in full sun. Bird grape is a slender, thin-barked native vine of Florida hammocks, pinelands, and Gulf Coast scrub, distinguished from the related muscadine by its smaller leaves and less shaggy bark, and it climbs readily by tendrils once given support. Its small, sweet black grapes ripen over a long season and are eaten avidly by songbirds, making it a valuable addition to a wildlife hedge or fence line rather than a fruit crop for the table. It tolerates the heat, humidity, sandy soils, and periodic drought of the Gulf Coast better than most grape species, needing only occasional pruning to keep it in bounds.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, sandy, well-drained to seasonally moist soil in full sun to partial shade; netted pawpaw is native to Florida and south Georgia pine flatwoods and scrub, where it forms low colonies from spreading roots.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, choosing a site that mimics the pine flatwoods and scrub where this pawpaw grows wild. Large, fragrant, creamy-white to maroon flowers open in spring before or alongside the new leaves, followed by yellow-green, custard-fleshed fruit that ripens smaller than common pawpaw but is sweet and edible fresh. The shrub spreads slowly by root suckers into low colonies and tolerates the sandy, low-fertility, seasonally wet-then-dry soils typical of the Gulf Coast pine belt far better than most fruiting shrubs. It is also a larval host for the zebra swallowtail butterfly, adding pollinator and wildlife value to a native fruit or naturalized planting.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

common_name: Winter Grape (Graybark Grape, Sweet Mountain Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a sturdy arbor or fence in well-drained bottomland or upland soil in full sun; this vigorous native grape ranges across the Gulf South's river bottoms and woodland edges.

directions: Plant dormant cuttings or bare-root vines against a sturdy arbor, fence, or trellis in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Winter grape is a vigorous, high-climbing native vine of river bottoms, thickets, and woodland edges across the Gulf South, bearing small, tart black grapes that ripen unusually late, often persisting on the vine into fall, which gives the plant its common name. Its dense, gray, felted young growth and strong disease and heat tolerance have made native populations valuable in grape breeding programs seeking rootstock resilient to Gulf Coast humidity and pests. In the home landscape it is best used as a screening or wildlife vine on a large arbor, since it grows quickly and needs annual pruning to control its size.

planting.note: Plant young container-grown trees in fall in wet, poorly drained, seasonally flooded soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina ash is a small wetland tree of swamps, sloughs, and pond margins across the Gulf Coastal Plain and tolerates prolonged standing water.

directions: Plant young container-grown trees in fall in wet to seasonally flooded, poorly drained soil in full sun to partial shade, since Carolina ash naturally roots in cypress-tupelo swamps, sloughs, and pond margins where standing water lingers for much of the year. It stays small compared to other native ashes, usually developing a multi-trunked, shrubby to small-tree form with glossy compound leaves, and its inflated, corky-winged seed pods float on floodwater to disperse, giving the tree its 'pop ash' nickname. Inconspicuous spring flowers provide early nectar for native bees before the leaves fully emerge, and the seeds are eaten by waterfowl and other wetland wildlife. It is a dependable small shade tree for the wettest corners of a Gulf Coast landscape, including pond edges, rain garden basins, and low spots that hold water after heavy rain.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America
